title: Headline labour resilience masks widening place-based differences in jobs, wages, skills, and bargaining conditions
source_unit: OECD, OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
geography: OECD countries, subnational regions, workers, households, firms, and local labour markets

unemployment_rate.unit: percent OECD unemployment rate in May 2026

employment_rate.unit: percent average OECD employment rate in Q1 2026

labour_force_participation.unit: percent average OECD labour-force participation rate in Q1 2026

resilience_boundary.value: headline employment and participation remain high while unemployment is rising slightly and growth is flattening

observations.method: OECD labour-market surveillance using national and OECD statistical indicators, recent employment and unemployment developments, and comparative policy analysis.
observations.uncertainty: OECD averages conceal country, region, age, occupation, contract, and household differences; low unemployment does not establish job quality, security, or bargaining power.
observations.subgroup: Young entrants, prime-age and older workers, migrants, firms, households, and workers in regions with different labour-market tightness.
observations.counterinterpretation: Record employment and low unemployment can represent real gains even when the pace of improvement slows or the distribution of gains is unequal.

observations.period: 2021-2026; real wages, energy shocks, and young labour-market entry

denominator.unit: OECD wage and labour-market comparison frame

real_wage_recovery.value: real wages remained below early-2021 levels in around one-third of OECD countries

young_entry_difficulty.value: young labour-market entrants face particular difficulties, with widening unemployment gaps in the countries analysed

ai_explanation_boundary.value: the role of recent large-language-model advances in young people’s difficulties appears limited in the evidence reviewed

energy_transmission.value: the 2026 energy shock is expected to put further pressure on wages

observations.method: OECD comparison of real wages, employment entry, unemployment gaps, labour-market tightness, and technology-related evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish one causal source for wage or youth-entry outcomes; energy, demand, skills, technology, demographics, and local labour-market conditions interact.
observations.subgroup: Young entrants, workers with different education levels, wage earners, energy-exposed sectors, and households whose purchasing room depends on real income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Wage recovery may resume as inflation and energy pressures ease, while targeted skills and employment policies can improve entry without treating AI as the sole explanation.

observations.period: 2000-2022; structural shocks and local labour-market divergence

denominator.unit: OECD countries in the report's linked employer-employee and regional structural-change analysis

shock_channels.value: trade, digitalisation, artificial intelligence, robotics, and the energy transition are reshaping local labour markets

place_divergence.value: some places emerge stronger while others experience persistent economic decline, producing divergent employment and well-being trajectories

distributional_endpoint.value: regional structural change affects workers, employers, and the economic fortunes of places differently

policy_endpoint.value: place-based labour-market, industrial, education, infrastructure, and social policies are needed alongside worker support

observations.method: OECD regional analysis of trade and technology shocks using linked employer-employee and local labour-market evidence across 14 countries, interpreted with broader regional policy synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-country analysis is not a universal causal estimate for every region and does not show that a particular policy package will reverse decline everywhere.
observations.subgroup: Lagging and leading regions, workers exposed to structural change, firms, local institutions, commuters, and households tied to place-specific job and service opportunities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Places can adapt through new industries, mobility, skills, infrastructure, and public investment; divergence is a risk pattern, not an irreversible destiny.

observations.period: 2026; skills, training, employment protection, and non-compete constraints

denominator.unit: OECD employment-policy and job-mobility synthesis frame

skills_returns.value: returns to skills depend on occupations, work practices, and training design rather than skills alone

noncompete.value: non-compete clauses are pervasive and have adverse effects on productivity and wages

protection_design.value: tailored employment-protection legislation can help labour markets navigate short-term fluctuations and structural change

institutional_route.value: skills policy, employment protection, worker mobility, and local economic development interact

observations.method: OECD comparative review of skills, training, employment protection, non-compete agreements, job mobility, and local labour-market policy.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not identify the effect of every clause or training programme in every occupation and does not directly observe worker bargaining or household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Workers changing jobs, workers in occupations with non-competes, employers, trainees, local governments, and institutions managing structural transitions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some restrictions can protect legitimate investment or trade secrets, and training can pay off when job design and institutions allow workers to use the acquired skills.

related_sources.claim: OECD chapter on local exposure to trade and technology shocks and place-based policy implications.
OECD release summarizing employment, unemployment, wage, and energy-shock findings.

boundary: This record adds a place-based labour-market route across headline resilience, real wages, young entry, structural shocks, skills, non-compete constraints, and employment policy. It uses OECD aggregate indicators, regional analysis, and report synthesis, not respondent-level employment histories, individual wage panels, private employer files, causal AI displacement estimates, or proof that a policy works uniformly across places.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD Employment Outlook 2026 landing page, full report, local-labour-market chapter, and press release reviewed for labour-market rates, wage recovery, youth entry, structural shocks, skills, non-competes, and policy boundaries.
